description: GeoFuego (geofuego.com.ar): live fire monitoring for Argentina - NASA FIRMS hotspots, a 2012-today fire calendar by province, and a seasonal risk index with published method (doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23017739, v1.2). Our goal: harmonize MODIS and VIIRS into one honest multi-decade fire calendar.
summary:
Argentina's satellite fire record is two records: MODIS since 2000 and VIIRS since 2012. VIIRS sees about three fire pixels where MODIS sees one, so the joined record shows a false jump in 2012 (2.3× nationally) and this season cannot be compared with 2008.

We built a harmonization engine that converts MODIS counts to VIIRS-equivalent counts with a factor per 0.25° cell, calendar month and satellite set, fitted on the days both sensors flew (2012–2023), and a web app on top of it. For a province, a point or an area drawn on the map, and any date range, it gives one burning-activity calendar from November 2000 to today: hotspots per month and year, anomalies, the current month against its history, rankings, and CSV and PNG downloads.

Every reconstructed month carries an 80 % range calibrated out of sample. On years the model never saw (2024 and 2025) national totals are predicted within 2–5 %; fire-season error is 3.2 % for the country and 9.8 % per province.

It matters now: Suomi NPP, the reference VIIRS satellite, stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026. The record already continues on NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 on the same scale. Code, data and validation are open, with a DOI.
details:
Links. App: https://spaceapps.geofuego.com.ar/ · Method and validation: https://spaceapps.geofuego.com.ar/method/ · Code and data: https://github.com/germankovacevic-lab/geofuego-harmonization · Archived release with DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24220107

What it does. One monthly fire-hotspot calendar for any area of Argentina, November 2000 to today, in a single unit (VIIRS-equivalent 375 m detections), so that the sensor of origin no longer matters. In the app the user selects an area (province, point by latitude/longitude, 0.25° cells clicked on the map, or a rectangle) and a date range, and gets:

  • the calendar year × month with the value in every cell, year totals and a median row, in Count or Anomaly mode (month ÷ median of the same month), with Fire, Viridis and Cividis colour scales (the last two colour-blind safe);
  • this month vs the historical median, month to date, plus the last complete month and the year to date;
  • which years and which months burned most; critical months, typical year and worst year;
  • a before/after panel for the selected area: the naive splice, MODIS alone and the harmonized series across 2012 (nationally ×2.33, ×0.74 and ×0.77), with a yearly table of the harmonized total, its range and the raw count of each satellite (MODIS Terra + Aqua, VIIRS S-NPP, and NOAA-20 / NOAA-21 for 2023–2025);
  • where the number comes from: the share of the hotspots in the selected dates that VIIRS observed, that was reconstructed from MODIS, and that is preliminary;
  • notable fire events as shareable links (Corrientes 2022, Córdoba 2020, Paraná Delta 2020, Comarca Andina 2021, Cholila 2015, Chilecito 2026), each with a NASA satellite image of the area before and after the fires (MODIS Terra false colour, from NASA Worldview / GIBS), so the peak in the calendar can be seen on the ground;
  • a year-by-year and month-by-month fire film on the map, for the selected area: the whole country, one province or any area drawn by the user;
  • five base maps, two of them from NASA GIBS (the VIIRS true-colour image of the previous day from NOAA-20, and the Black Marble night lights), and a full-screen map;
  • CSV downloads (monthly values of the area with range, sensor of origin and quality flags; one row per 0.25° cell and month with hotspots; the yearly table per satellite) and a PNG of the calendar;
  • a Method & validation page inside the app (unit, factor, fixed heat sources, bridge to NOAA-20/21, validation with its negative results, declared limits); English and Spanish.

How it works. (1) NASA FIRMS country archives: MODIS Terra and Aqua 2000–2025 and VIIRS S-NPP 2012–2025, 4.6 million detections over Argentina. (2) Fixed heat sources (gas flares, industry, and MODIS summer false alarms on hot bare ground) are separated into their own class of 1 628 cells of 0.02° and kept as a separate series, never mixed with vegetation fire. (3) A VIIRS/MODIS factor per 0.25° cell × calendar month × satellite set (Terra + Aqua; Terra alone for November 2000 – June 2002), computed as a ratio of sums on the days both sensors flew in 2012–2023, with hierarchical shrinkage from cell to province, fire-regime region and country where a cell has too little data. (4) Satellite outages are detected and filled across sensors, and checked against NASA mission records. (5) An 80 % prediction range, asymmetric, calibrated on out-of-sample residuals by region, size of the area and predicted count, widened in strong ENSO months and in months cloudier than usual (ERA5 cloud fraction at the overpass hour). (6) A bridge from S-NPP to NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 (0.979 / 0.951, fitted on the days all three reported in 2023–2025) so the series continues on the newer satellites now that Suomi NPP stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026; the 2026 months are shown as a preliminary near-real-time layer, outside the harmonized record.

How we know it works (all out of sample). Leave-one-year-out 2012–2023, fire-season error: country 3.2 %, province 9.8 %, single cell 30 % (one national factor: 8.9 / 15.0 / 34 %). Years never used, 2024 and 2025: national predicted/observed 1.044 and 1.024; the 80 % range holds 80 % / 77 % of cell-months and 76 % / 73 % of province-months. The ratio drifts about 3 % between 2012–17 and 2018–23. Across the 2012 splice, burned hectares per hotspot (MCD64A1) stay at 0.98 with the harmonized series against 3.12 with the naive concatenation. Hypotheses we measured and rejected are documented with their numbers: ENSO as a correction of the factor, separate day and night factors, an additive term for months where MODIS saw nothing.

Limits we declare. Nothing independent of MODIS validates 2000–2011: the reconstruction is right to the degree that the 2012–2023 relation held before. Small areas still show the sensor change (MODIS missed small fires), so the app applies size tiers and marks pre-2012 zeros as "no MODIS detection". Counts are satellite detections, not fires and not burned area. A cloudy month reads low (flagged, not corrected).

Benefits and intended impact. Emergency managers, scientists and land managers see 26 years instead of 14 and can compare the current season with every season since 2000, with an honest margin of error and a record that does not jump when the satellite changes. It is what the challenge asks for: the sensor of origin no longer matters, and the patterns, trends and anomalies become the focus — which periods of the year burn, which years burned most and how the current month compares with the historical median, for the area each user chooses.

What is creative, and what we considered. The factor is not one national number: it changes with place, calendar month and satellite set, and it is shrunk towards the region where data are thin. Fixed heat sources are a class of their own instead of noise. Every reconstructed month says how far it can be trusted, and that range was tested on two years kept aside. The splice of 2012 is checked against an independent product (burned area). And the method already crosses the next change of satellite: Suomi NPP stopped this month and the series continues on NOAA-20 and NOAA-21.

Tools. JavaScript (Node.js 20) for the whole data pipeline and the web app; Python 3 (numpy, matplotlib, netCDF4, cdsapi) for ERA5 and the figures; Leaflet, Leaflet.draw and uPlot (vendored) in the browser; Cloudflare Pages for static hosting (no server, no database); Git/GitHub; Zenodo for the DOI. No hardware.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI). We used Claude (Anthropic) intensively: SI wrote most of the code under the team's direction, ran the analyses, drafted and edited the English text, tested the app and reviewed the method in isolated sessions (reports published in the repository and labelled as SI-produced). The idea — a regional, calendar-month factor instead of a national scalar, carried from 2000 to the present — is the team's and predates the hackathon; the SI reviews proposed, the team decided, and every proposal was measured before being adopted or rejected. SI assistance is acknowledged in the README, in CITATION.cff, in the header of every script, in the headers of the published data files and in the app footer. No figure, chart, map or data value is SI-generated: all are produced by our scripts from NASA FIRMS data. The two videos (30-second demo in English; three-minute presentation in Spanish) are presented by an SI-generated character, Max: still image SI-generated, lip-sync with Hedra, voice with ElevenLabs. A visible label is on screen while he appears, and the About page, the video descriptions and the file metadata say it in text. No NASA branding is used in any generated content.

Pre-hackathon work (disclosure). What existed before the hackathon window opened (14 Nov 2026, 09:00 ART): (a) GeoFuego (https://geofuego.com.ar), our live fire-monitoring platform, and its published method package (GeoFuego Index v1.2, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24164911), including the province-to-region table we reuse; (b) a written method design (13 Nov) and a submission plan; (c) a preliminary feasibility check of the MODIS/VIIRS ratio run in Sept–Nov 2026 on the public FIRMS archives, used to decide that the approach was worth building; (d) the public FIRMS archives already downloaded, the vendored front-end libraries, and an empty placeholder page at spaceapps.geofuego.com.ar (13 Nov); (e) the team's dataset Estado hídrico de la Argentina 2001–2026 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24035880), quoted in one context line of the app for 2026. All code in the repository, every dataset, figure, validation and document was written inside the window (first commit 14 Nov 09:04 ART). The feasibility numbers are not reused: the repository recomputes everything from the raw data.
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS country archives: MODIS Collection 6/6.1 (Terra, Aqua) 2000–2025 and VIIRS 375 m S-NPP (VNP14IMG) 2012–2025 — the base of the record and the overlap on which every factor is fitted
NASA FIRMS Area API: VIIRS S-NPP, NOAA-20 (VJ114IMG) and NOAA-21 (VJ214IMG), standard processing 2023–2025 (satellite bridge) and near real time 2026 (preliminary current year)
NASA Worldview Snapshots: MODIS Terra corrected reflectance, bands 7-2-1, before and after each of the six notable fire events (context only)
NASA GIBS (Global Imagery Browse Services): VIIRS NOAA-20 true colour of the previous day and Black Marble night lights, two base maps of the app
NASA MODAPS: Terra data outage table (check of the satellite outages our detector finds)
NASA MODAPS: Aqua data outage table
NASA Earthdata: data alerts and outages (Suomi NPP stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026)
MODIS burned area MCD64A1 v061 (through the GWIS country tables): consistency check across the 2012 splice
MODIS vegetation index MOD13A3 v061 (through the team's pre-existing dataset Estado hídrico de la Argentina): one context line for 2026
Giglio, Schroeder & Justice (2016), The Collection 6 MODIS active fire detection algorithm and fire products, Remote Sensing of Environment 178
Schroeder, Oliva, Giglio & Csiszar (2014), The New VIIRS 375 m active fire detection data product, Remote Sensing of Environment 143
